events.title: Judge Cooley calls personal immunity a right “to be let alone”
events.place: University of Michigan Law Department, Ann Arbor, Michigan (published by Callaghan & Company, Chicago)
events.summary: Judge Thomas M. Cooley of the University of Michigan published A Treatise on the Law of Torts with Callaghan & Company of Chicago; his preface is dated Ann Arbor, December 1878 and the first edition bears the date 1879. events.title: Punch cards count the 1890 US census
events.place: U.S. Census Office, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: In a test run for the Census Office in 1889, Herman Hollerith's punch-card system transcribed data from four St. Louis enumeration districts in 72.5 hours and tabulated it in 5.5 hours; his two rivals needed 144.5 and 100.5 hours just to transcribe. Hollerith, whose electro-mechanical tabulating machine had been patented on 8 January 1889, won the contract to supply tabulators for the 1890 census. Clerks punched each person's answers into cards that the machine read electrically, and census clerks tabulated data for nearly 63 million people this way. Hollerith founded the Tabulating Machine Company in 1896; a 1911 merger folded it into the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company, which was renamed International Business Machines (IBM) in 1924.
events.significance: The census became the first mass machine-readable record of individuals — the technical root of every later databank and data-protection fight.

events.title: Warren and Brandeis argue for a legal “right to privacy”
events.place: Harvard Law Review, Harvard Law School, Cambridge, Massachusetts
events.summary: Samuel D. Warren, a Boston paper manufacturer who had recently left the law, and his former law partner Louis D. Brandeis published “The Right to Privacy” in the Harvard Law Review, vol. IV, no. 5, dated 15 December 1890 (4 Harv. L. Rev. 193). Citing “what Judge Cooley calls the right ‘to be let alone’”, they warned that “instantaneous photographs and newspaper enterprise have invaded the sacred precincts of private and domestic life”. They argued that the common law already secured each person's right to decide “to what extent his thoughts, sentiments, and emotions shall be communicated to others”.
events.significance: It reframed privacy from walls and property to a person's control over what is communicated about them — the seed of every later consent regime.

events.title: Georgia's Supreme Court recognises a right of privacy

events.title: US census law bars using returns against the people who gave them
events.place: United States Congress, U.S. Capitol, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: Earlier census acts had required that census information “shall be used only for the statistical purposes for which it is supplied” (1909) and that only sworn census employees examine individual reports (the act for the 1920 census). The act providing for the Fifteenth Census, approved 18 June 1929, was the first census law to extend the no-identification promise to individuals: “No publication shall be made by the Census Office whereby the data furnished by any particular establishment or individual can be identified.” As the Census Bureau read it, the act also protected the information from being used “to the detriment of the person or persons to whom such information relates”. Congress codified the 1929 law in 1954 as Title 13 of the U.S. Code, which carries virtually the same language.
events.significance: An early statutory purpose-limitation promise: data given for counting may not be turned against the giver — a promise that would be broken within 13 years.

It also leaves out the 1929 act's main novelty, which its own source records: it was 'the first to extend the promise to individuals', i.e. 'No publication shall be made by the Census Office whereby the data furnished by any particular establishment or individual can be identified'.

The 'to the detriment of the person or persons to whom such information relates' wording is attributed by Ruggles & Magnuson to how 'the Census Bureau further clarified' the 1929 act. The 13 U.S.C. § 8 derivation notes (Cornell LII) trace the later 'detriment' proviso to the transcript section of the 1929 act (June 18, 1929, ch. 28, § 18, 46 Stat. 25), so it is narrower than a general bar. The corrected wording attributes the reading to the Bureau.

The 1954 Title 13 codification is confirmed by the Census Bureau's own 2001 monograph (added). The significance claim about wartime breach is supported by the same article (Second War Powers Act 1942; wartime disclosures documented by Seltzer and Anderson 2007).

events.title: Nazi census asks about Jewish grandparents — under a promise of statistical secrecy
events.place: Statistisches Reichsamt (Statistical Office of the Reich), Berlin
events.summary: Germany's census of 17 May 1939 came with a supplementary card for each household asking whether any grandparent was Jewish, where the 16 June 1933 census had asked about religion. Respondents were threatened with heavy penalties for false answers but promised discretion (cards in a sealed envelope) and “a purely statistical evaluation”. Cards recording a Jewish grandparent were nonetheless passed, after statistical processing, to the Reich Office of Genealogy. The surviving cards list about 277,500 people classed as of Jewish origin, in about 130,000 households, with names, birth dates and exact addresses. The Federal Archives says it has not been proved that the cards were used to prepare the deportations, and thinks it unlikely: they reached the registration offices only in April/May 1941 and the Genealogy Office in January 1942.
events.significance: A census confidentiality promise was broken. “Racial” data collected for “a purely statistical evaluation” ended up, by name and address, in a Nazi genealogy office. Once data is collected, a promise to keep statistical and identifying data apart is only as strong as the regime holding it.

sources.institution: Bundesarchiv (German Federal Archives), Nicolai M. Zimmermann
sources.title: The supplementary cards stating information about origin and educational background of the population census of 17 May 1939
sources.quote: In order to obtain correct details, massive penalties were threatened on the one hand while on the other hand discretion of those counting was officially assured; the counters were to receive the cards in a sealed envelope. They also promised a purely statistical evaluation.
sources.note: Undated archive essay (date = access date). Same essay: 'Provided that one of the household members had answered the question asking for a Jewish grandparent with yes, the supplementary cards were brought – after their regular evaluation by the Statistical Authority of the Reich, the State Statistical Offices and the registry offices of the police – to the Reich Office of Genealogy' and 'approximately 130,000 households ... approximately 277,500 citizens with their full name, date and place of birth, their origin as well as their precise address as per deadline 17 May 1939'.

sources.institution: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, Holocaust Encyclopedia
sources.title: Locating the Victims
sources.quote: Aggregated census data processed by Hollerith machines could provide the Nazi government with information on how many Jews lived in a particular German city, since the census of 1939 included data on “race,” identifying who was a Jew as defined by the Nuremberg Laws.
sources.note: USHMM stresses that location and identification of victims 'did not rely on modern technology, as sometimes claimed in the popular media' — see the myth record.

events.locationNote: Coordinates are central Berlin; the Statistisches Reichsamt's exact building is not verified.

issues: The significance overstates the source. It says the census 'extract[ed] exactly the data that fed persecution', which implies the cards were used to find Jews for deportation. The cited Bundesarchiv essay says the opposite. Their use for the deportations 'could not be proved so far ... and is rather unlikely', because the cards reached the registration offices only in April/May 1941 and the Reich Office of Genealogy only from January 1942. The USHMM source also stresses that census data served in aggregate and that identifying victims 'did not rely on modern technology'. The significance is rewritten so it keeps what is documented (a broken 'purely statistical' promise; identifying racial data sent to a Nazi genealogy office) without claiming the cards drove deportations.

Summary: 'the surviving cards name about 277,500 people' is imprecise. The essay counts about 277,500 people of Jewish origin under the Nazi classification, in about 130,000 households. The cards covered everyone in a household, so they also record many non-Jewish people (Table 1: 410,920 people in total on the cards passed on). Reworded.

Checked OK: census date 17 May 1939; the 16 June 1933 census asked about religion; a supplementary card for each household; 'massive penalties' threatened; sealed envelope; 'purely statistical evaluation'; cards with a Jewish grandparent passed to the Reich Office of Genealogy after statistical processing. Central-Berlin coordinates are fine (flagged in locationNote).

events.title: A model Dutch population register becomes a tool of deportation
events.place: Rijksinspectie van de Bevolkingsregisters (State Inspectorate of Population Registers), The Hague
events.summary: Before the German occupation the Netherlands had completed a comprehensive population registration system, praised by statistics chief H. W. Methorst in 1938 for following each person “from cradle to grave”. By early 1941 his successor as head of the registration office, J. L. Lentz, had adapted it into special registers of Jews and Roma (“Gypsies”). These registers and the related identity cards played an important role in rounding them up before deportation. Dutch Jews had the highest death rate (73 percent) of Jews in any occupied western European country. Jewish refugees living in the Netherlands died at a lower rate. Demographers William Seltzer and Margo Anderson think the best explanation is that, unlike most Dutch Jews, the refugees avoided registration.
events.significance: It showed that an accurate, centralised, linked register is dangerous in itself: the harm came from data built for benign administration, once control over it changed hands.

sources.institution: Social Research (William Seltzer and Margo Anderson), Johns Hopkins University Press
sources.title: The Dark Side of Numbers: The Role of Population Data Systems in Human Rights Abuses
sources.quote: These registration systems and the related identity cards played an important role in the apprehension of Dutch Jews and Gypsies prior to their eventual deportation to the death camps.
sources.note: Social Research 68(2), Summer 2001, pp. 481-513, at 487-488 (JSTOR stable URL https://www.jstor.org/stable/40971467). Read from a copy posted for a University of Washington course (CSDE 502). Same page: 'By early 1941 Methorst's successor as head of the population registration office, J. L. Lentz, had quickly adapted this general "cradle to grave" system to create special registration systems covering the Jewish and Gypsy populations' and 'Dutch Jews had the highest death rate (73 percent) of Jews residing in any occupied western European country'. They explain the refugees' lower death rate by the fact that they 'avoided registration'. Seltzer's fuller treatment (Population and Development Review 24(3), 1998) was not read.

It cites Loe de Jong and Presser. It also says Lentz set up, at Berlin's request, a shadow archive in The Hague of every identity card, which supports the Hague location.

Seltzer and Anderson say that Jewish refugees from Germany and other countries living in the Netherlands had a lower death rate than Dutch Jews. They offer as the 'best explanation' that the refugees, 'unlike most Dutch Jews, avoided registration'. That is their interpretation, not an established fact, so the summary now attributes it.

Lentz is his successor as head of the registration office. By early 1941 there were special registers of Jews and 'Gypsies'. The identity cards played 'an important role'. The death rate was 73 percent. Page numbers 487-488 match the running heads. An independent check (nl.wikipedia, Jacobus Lambertus Lentz) confirms that Lentz headed the Rijksinspectie van de Bevolkingsregisters (The Hague), set up under the 1936 decree requiring a personal card for every inhabitant from 1 July 1936, and 'speelde ook een hoofdrol in de uitvoering van de aanmeldplicht voor Joden'.

events.title: Wartime law lifts census confidentiality; data on Japanese Americans handed over
events.place: U.S. Bureau of the Census / Department of Commerce, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: From January 1942 the Census Bureau helped the Army on the West Coast remove Japanese Americans. It supplied tract-level tabulations and census-block maps showing how many Japanese Americans lived on each block. The Second War Powers Act (March 1942) then let the Secretary of Commerce supply census information for the conduct of the war, suspending census confidentiality. In 2007 historian Margo Anderson and statistician William Seltzer showed from Commerce Department records that the Bureau had complied, within seven days, with a 4 August 1943 request from Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau. He had asked for the names and locations of all people of Japanese ancestry in the Washington, D.C., area. Congress restored census confidentiality in 1947.
events.significance: The textbook case of data collected under a confidentiality promise being repurposed against the people who supplied it — the reason purpose limits must bind the data, not just the collector's good intentions.

sources.institution: Scientific American (JR Minkel)
sources.title: Confirmed: The U.S. Census Bureau Gave Up Names of Japanese-Americans in WW II
sources.quote: A new study of U.S. Department of Commerce documents now shows that the Census Bureau complied with an August 4, 1943, request by Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau for the names and locations of all people of Japanese ancestry in the Washington, D.C., area, according to historian Margo Anderson of the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee and statistician William Seltzer of Fordham University in New York City.
sources.note: Same article: 'The Second War Powers Act of 1942 temporarily repealed that protection to assist in the roundup of Japanese-Americans for imprisonment in internment camps in California and six other states during the war.' / 'The newly revealed documents show that census officials released the information just seven days after it was requested.' / 'Lawmakers restored the confidentiality of census data in 1947.' The underlying paper is W. Seltzer and M. Anderson, 'Census Confidentiality under the Second War Powers Act (1942-1947)', Population Association of America annual meeting, New York, 29-31 March 2007 (not read directly).

sources.title: “It's None of Their Damn Business”: Privacy and Disclosure Control in the U.S. Census, 1790–2020
sources.quote: The passage of the Second War Powers Act (1942) stated that the Secretary of Commerce, at the discretion of the President, was permitted to “make such special investigations and reports of census or statistical matters as may be needed in connection with the conduct of the war”
sources.note: Same passage: 'Seltzer and Anderson (2007) documented multiple examples of wartime disclosure of individual-level census responses.' Statute cited as Second War Powers Act 1942, Title XIV, §1402, 56 Stat. 186.

sources.institution: Social Research (William Seltzer and Margo Anderson), Johns Hopkins University Press
sources.title: The Dark Side of Numbers: The Role of Population Data Systems in Human Rights Abuses
sources.quote: The Census Bureau also gave direct assistance to the military authorities on the West Coast by: (1) providing tract-level tabulations of Japanese Americans from the 1940 Census in January 1942
sources.note: Social Research 68(2), Summer 2001, p. 492 (JSTOR stable URL https://www.jstor.org/stable/40971467), read from a course copy. --check FOUND. The same list continues (FOUND): '(3) making available census-block maps showing the number of Japanese American enumerated as residing in each block'. Also FOUND, p. 498: 'Yet even before the Second War Powers Act was introduced in Congress early in 1942, the director of the Census Bureau indicated his willingness to ignore the law so as to provide defense authorities a way of checking confidential census information on individual Japanese Americans'.

events.locationNote: Census Bureau headquarters in Washington (it moved to Suitland, Maryland, during the war); coordinates are the Commerce Department building, whose chief clerk authorised the releases.

issues: Wrong states. The summary says the Census Bureau 'provided block-level data locating Japanese Americans in California and six other states'. This repeats a Scientific American sentence that lists California, Arizona, Wyoming, Colorado, Utah, Idaho and Arkansas. Those are the seven states that held the War Relocation Authority camps, and SciAm's own earlier sentence uses them for 'internment camps in California and six other states'. They are not where Japanese Americans lived before removal. Washington and Oregon, which had large pre-war communities, are missing from the list. Seltzer and Anderson's own peer-reviewed account (Social Research 2001, p. 492) says the Bureau helped 'the military authorities on the West Coast', with tract-level tabulations in January 1942 and census-block maps of Japanese Americans per block.

Misleading sequence. The summary puts the block-level help after the Second War Powers Act (March 1942), implying the Act enabled it. The tract tabulations date from January 1942, before the Act. Seltzer and Anderson also note that before the Act was even introduced, the Census director said he was willing to ignore the law to let defense authorities check individual census records.

events.title: Universal Declaration makes privacy a human right (Article 12)
events.place: Palais de Chaillot, Paris (UN General Assembly, third session)
events.summary: The UN General Assembly, meeting in Paris, proclaimed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948 (resolution 217 A). Article 12 provides that “no one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence” and that everyone has the right to the protection of the law against such interference.
events.significance: Privacy moved from national tort law into the universal vocabulary of human rights, framed as protection against arbitrary interference by others.

sources.institution: United Nations
sources.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
sources.quote: No one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence, nor to attacks upon his honour and reputation. Everyone has the right to the protection of the law against such interference or attacks.
sources.note: Same page: 'the Declaration was proclaimed by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 ( General Assembly resolution 217 A )'.

events.locationNote: The third session of the General Assembly met at the Palais de Chaillot, Paris (venue from general knowledge; the UN page says only 'in Paris').

issues: No errors found. The Article 12 text is verbatim. 10 December 1948, Paris, resolution 217 A are confirmed on the UN page (the UN 'History of the Declaration' page gives '217 A (III) of 10 December 1948, the General Assembly, meeting in Paris'). The Palais de Chaillot venue is not on the UN pages, but en.wikipedia 'Palais de Chaillot' confirms 'It is in the Chaillot Palace that the UNGA adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948'. Coordinates match the Palais de Chaillot.

events.title: European Convention guarantees respect for private and family life (Article 8)
events.place: Palazzo Barberini, Rome
events.summary: Members of the Council of Europe signed the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms in Rome on 4 November 1950. Article 8 gives everyone “the right to respect for his private and family life, his home and his correspondence”, and allows interference by a public authority only when “in accordance with the law” and “necessary in a democratic society” for listed aims.
events.significance: Unlike the UDHR, Article 8 is enforceable by a court; its tests of legality and necessity became the frame for Europe's later data-protection law.

sources.title: Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (as amended)

sources.note: Article 8(1). events.title: East Germany creates the Ministry for State Security (Stasi)
events.place: Volkskammer (People's Chamber), East Berlin
events.summary: On 8 February 1950 the GDR's Volkskammer passed, in a rushed procedure, a law turning the Interior Ministry's Main Administration for the Protection of the Economy into the Ministry for State Security. It took effect when President Wilhelm Pieck promulgated it on 18 February. In 1989 the ministry had 91,015 full-time employees (as of 31 October) and about 189,000 unofficial informers, one for every 89 citizens. Its surviving records run to more than 111 kilometres of files.
events.significance: The Stasi became the reference case for total surveillance by file and informer — and, after 1990, for a person's right to see what the state had recorded about them.

sources.note: Translation: 'On 8 February 1950 a Volkskammer law was passed in an expedited procedure that separated the Main Administration for the Protection of the Economy from the GDR Ministry of the Interior and upgraded it to the Ministry for State Security.' events.title: Prosser sorts seventy years of privacy cases into four torts
events.place: University of California School of Law (Boalt Hall), Berkeley, California
events.summary: In “Privacy”, California Law Review vol. 48 no. 3 (August 1960), p. 383, Dean William L. Prosser of the University of California School of Law surveyed the case law since Warren and Brandeis. He concluded it was “not one tort, but a complex of four”: intrusion upon seclusion, public disclosure of embarrassing private facts, false-light publicity, and appropriation of name or likeness. Law professor Amy Gajda credits the article with substantially boosting the influence of Warren and Brandeis's essay, which courts cited far more often after 1960 than before.
events.significance: Prosser's four torts are all after-the-fact remedies for harm — privacy as a lawsuit, not as terms a person sets in advance.

Publicity which places the plaintiff in a false light in the public eye. 4. Appropriation, for the defendant's advantage, of the plaintiff's name or likeness.' events.title: Vance Packard's The Naked Society sounds the alarm on surveillance
events.place: David McKay Company, New York City
events.summary: Journalist Vance Packard, author of The Hidden Persuaders, published The Naked Society (New York: David McKay, 1964), a popular exposé whose first part is titled “The Mounting Surveillance”. It opens by looking in on “a reasonably successful family in a typical city of the Land of Liberty, 1964”, who are watched at every turn. The mother is recorded by a closed-circuit TV camera hidden behind a mesh screen in a store dressing room. On 26 July 1966 Packard was the first witness when a House subcommittee on invasion of privacy opened hearings on proposals for a National Data Center.
events.significance: It helped carry privacy out of the law reviews to a general readership worried about files, bugs and hidden cameras. Two years later lawmakers weighing a federal data bank called its author as their first witness.

The hearings were held by the House Committee on Government Operations' Special Subcommittee on Invasion of Privacy (Chairman Cornelius E. Gallagher), not by Congress as a whole. The record confirms that the subcommittee 'today begins its investigation into proposals to establish a National Data Center or Data Bank' on 26 July 1966, and Gallagher calls Packard 'its first witness in this series of hearings'.

events.title: Griswold v. Connecticut finds “zones of privacy” in the Constitution
events.place: Supreme Court of the United States, 1 First Street NE, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: Planned Parenthood League of Connecticut's executive director and its medical director had been convicted for advising married couples on contraception under a state law banning contraceptive use. On 7 June 1965 the Supreme Court struck the law down. Justice Douglas, for the Court, wrote that “specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights have penumbras” and that “various guarantees create zones of privacy”, which the ban on use by married couples violated.
events.significance: The US Constitution never mentions privacy. Griswold inferred a right of privacy from the “penumbras” of the Bill of Rights, protecting an intimate relationship, marriage, and not just property or places. Later cases built a wider right to make personal decisions on this footing.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States (U.S. Reports, Library of Congress)
sources.title: Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479 (1965)

sources.note: 381 U.S. at 484 (Douglas, J., for the Court). Syllabus: 'Argued March 29-30, 1965.-Decided June 7, 1965.' and 'The Connecticut statute forbidding use of contraceptives violates the right of marital privacy which is within the penumbra of specific guarantees of the Bill of Rights.' The scan's OCR scrambles the next sentence across columns, so it is quoted from the LII copy below.

It rests the right on the marital relationship and on place-based guarantees: the Third Amendment's 'in any house', the Fourth Amendment's 'persons, houses, papers, and effects', and 'Would we allow the police to search the sacred precincts of marital bedrooms ...?'. The autonomy reading came in later cases. Reworded to what the opinion says.

events.title: Congress puts the proposed National Data Center on trial
events.place: Room 2247, Rayburn House Office Building, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: In April 1965 a Social Science Research Council committee chaired by Yale economist Richard Ruggles urged a federal data bank, and a Bureau of the Budget task force under Carl Kaysen was studying access to government statistics. On 26–28 July 1966 the House Special Subcommittee on Invasion of Privacy, chaired by Rep. Cornelius Gallagher, held hearings on “The Computer and Invasion of Privacy”. Gallagher said the thought of Americans' records “neatly bundled together into one compact package is appalling” and suggested that a new concept in file accessibility might be needed, under which “a person may have the right to examine his own file”. Extensive press coverage of the hearings fed a growing national backlash against the plan.
events.significance: The databank fight produced an early official call for a person's right to examine their own file and challenge its accuracy. That is a seed of access rights, and of the idea that individuals, not just institutions, should hold the controls.

events.title: Katz: “the Fourth Amendment protects people, not places”
events.place: Supreme Court of the United States, 1 First Street NE, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: FBI agents had recorded Katz's side of telephone calls transmitting wagering information from Los Angeles to Miami and Boston by attaching an electronic listening device to the outside of the public telephone booth he used; the appeals court found no violation because there was no physical entrance. On 18 December 1967 the Supreme Court held that this was a search: “the Fourth Amendment protects people, not places”, and the “trespass” doctrine of Olmstead was “no longer controlling”. Justice Harlan's concurrence set out a two-part test: an actual expectation of privacy that “society is prepared to recognize as ‘reasonable’”.
events.significance: Katz vindicated Brandeis's 1928 dissent and cut privacy loose from walls — but tied it to 'reasonable expectations', a standard that shrinks as surveillance becomes normal.

sources.institution: Supreme Court of the United States (U.S. Reports, Library of Congress)
sources.title: Katz v. United States, 389 U.S. 347 (1967)
sources.quote: For the Fourth Amendment protects people, not places.
sources.note: 389 U.S. at 351 (Stewart, J., for the Court). Syllabus: 'Argued October 17, 1967.-Decided December 18, 1967.' and FBI agents 'had attached an electronic listening and recording device to the outside of the telephone booth from which the calls were made'. Harlan, J., concurring, at 361: 'there is a twofold requirement, first that a person have exhibited an actual (subjective) expectation of privacy and, second, that the expectation be one that society is prepared to recognize as "reasonable."' Opinion: 'the "trespass" doctrine there enunciated can no longer be regarded as controlling.' Opinion: the indictment charged him 'with transmitting wagering information by telephone from Los Angeles to Miami and Boston'.

events.locationNote: The Supreme Court Building, Washington.

issues: No error found. One nuance: the words 'no longer controlling' appear in the Syllabus ('is no longer controlling'). The opinion itself says 'can no longer be regarded as controlling'. Both are on the cited page, so the fragment is accurate. It concerns Olmstead and Goldman.

events.title: Title III sets warrant rules for wiretaps and bugs
events.place: United States Congress, U.S. Capitol, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: Title III of the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968 (Public Law 90-351, approved 19 June 1968) made it a federal crime to intercept wire and oral communications without authorisation. Officers could intercept with a court order, or where one party to the conversation consented, with a 48-hour emergency window before an order had to be sought. The Act also said nothing in it limited the President's constitutional power to take national-security measures. Congress found that “there has been extensive wiretapping carried on without legal sanctions, and without the consent of any of the parties to the conversation”, and that uniform rules were needed “to protect effectively the privacy of wire and oral communications”.
events.significance: Title III made consent of a party, or a judge's order, the normal gate for interception. This consent-or-warrant structure was later extended to electronic communications, though national-security wiretaps were left outside it.

Sec. 801(b): '(b) In order to protect effectively the privacy of wire and oral communications, to protect the integrity of court and administrative proceedings, and to prevent the obstruction of interstate commerce, it is necessary for Congress to define on a uniform basis the circumstances and conditions under which the interception of wire and oral ...'. Header: 'PUBLIC LAW 90-351-JUNE 19, 1968'. Short title: 'Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968'. OCR of scanned Statutes at Large.

sources.quote: shall limit the constitutional power of the President to take such measures as he deems necessary to protect the Nation against actual or potential attack or other hostile acts of a foreign power
sources.note: --check FOUND. This is the national-security carve-out cited in the corrected summary. The full sentence begins 'Nothing contained in this chapter or in section 605 of the Communications Act of 1934 ...'.

sources.note: --check FOUND (the space before the comma is as on the page). This independent source confirms the 19 June 1968 date. The next item, 'prohibits the unauthorized, nonconsensual interception of "wire, oral, or electronic communications" by government agencies as well as private parties', is also FOUND. It describes the Act as amended, including ECPA's 'electronic'.

issues: The summary overstates: it says Title III 'let police intercept only with a court order'. The Act as enacted also let officers intercept without an order where they were a party or 'one of the parties to the communication has given prior consent' (§2511(2)(c)). It allowed emergency interception without an order if an application was made 'within forty-eight hours' (§2518(7)). And it said nothing in it 'shall limit the constitutional power of the President' to take national-security measures (§2511(3)). All three are FOUND in the cited statute.

The significance calls it 'The first comprehensive US surveillance statute'. No source supports the superlative. The Communications Act of 1934, s. 605, already banned interception and divulgence, and Title III left national-security surveillance outside its rules. Reworded.
The date is right: 19 June 1968 (header 'PUBLIC LAW 90-351-JUNE 19, 1968'; BJA gives '6/19/68'). The findings quotes are verbatim.

events.title: Germany's Constitutional Court: the state may not catalogue the whole person
events.place: Bundesverfassungsgericht (Federal Constitutional Court), Karlsruhe
events.summary: A Bavarian woman who refused to answer the microcensus's 60 questions was fined 100 Deutschmarks. When she contested the fine, the Fürstenfeldbruck local court asked the Federal Constitutional Court whether the compulsory questions on holiday travel were constitutional. On 16 July 1969 (1 BvL 19/63) the First Senate upheld those questions. But it held that it would violate human dignity for the state to claim the right “to register and catalogue a person compulsorily in their whole personality”, even anonymously in a statistical survey. Each person must retain an “inner space” where, quoting the jurist Wintrich, “one is left in peace”.
events.significance: A direct line from the 'right to be let alone' to European data protection: it limited what the state may compile about a person, the precursor of the 1983 census judgment and informational self-determination.

sources.institution: Bundesverfassungsgericht (text via Deutschsprachiges Fallrecht, University of Bern)
sources.title: BVerfGE 27, 1 – Mikrozensus, Beschluss des Ersten Senats vom 16. Juli 1969, 1 BvL 19/63
sources.quote: Mit der Menschenwürde wäre es nicht zu vereinbaren, wenn der Staat das Recht für sich in Anspruch nehmen könnte, den Menschen zwangsweise in seiner ganzen Persönlichkeit zu registrieren und zu katalogisieren, sei es auch in der Anonymität einer statistischen Erhebung, und ihn damit wie eine Sache zu behandeln, die einer Bestandsaufnahme in jeder Beziehung zugänglich ist.
sources.note: Translation: 'It would be incompatible with human dignity if the state could claim the right to register and catalogue a person compulsorily in their entire personality, even in the anonymity of a statistical survey, and thereby treat them like a thing open to inventory in every respect.' Next paragraph: the individual must keep an 'Innenraum' ... 'in dem man in Ruhe gelassen wird und ein Recht auf Einsamkeit genießt' ('where one is left in peace and enjoys a right to solitude'), quoting Wintrich (1957). Facts: the respondent refused to answer 'alle 60 Fragen' and was fined 'eine Geldbuße von 100 DM'. Tenor: the microcensus provisions 'waren mit dem Grundgesetz vereinbar'. The court's own website does not publish pre-1998 decisions in full.

events.locationNote: The Court moved into its building at Schlossbezirk 3, Karlsruhe, in 1969; coordinates are that building.

issues: The summary says the woman 'challenged the statistics law'. She did not. She refused the enumerators and 'alle 60 Fragen', was fined 100 DM, and applied for a court ruling on the fine. The Amtsgericht Fürstenfeldbruck then stayed the case and referred the question to the Federal Constitutional Court ('hat das Amtsgericht Fürstenfeldbruck die Sache ausgesetzt und dem Bundesverfassungsgericht zur Entscheidung darüber vorgelegt'). That is a judicial referral (concrete norm review, hence 'BvL'). It was the local court that argued the compulsory holiday-travel questions violated Arts. 1 and 2 of the Basic Law.

The remaining claims are confirmed: 16 July 1969, 1 BvL 19/63, First Senate, the tenor upholding the holiday-travel questions, the dignity passage and the Wintrich 'Innenraum' quotation. The locationNote holds: German Wikipedia's Baumgarten-Bau article gives the key handover as 6 May 1969, 'Seit Mai 1969 dient der Baumgarten-Bau als Amtssitz', so the court was in the new building by 16 July 1969. The coordinates are within about 110 m of the article's coordinates (49°0'46"N 8°24'5"E).

By Amy Gajda's count, only about eighty cases mentioned the article by name between 1890 and 1960, against more than 400 in 1960–2007, after Prosser's restatement.

myths.claim: The US Census Bureau only released neighbourhood-level statistics on Japanese Americans in the Second World War, never names.
myths.correction: For decades the Census Bureau denied giving other agencies individual “microdata”. By 2000 it had acknowledged, and director Kenneth Prewitt had apologised for, releasing neighbourhood-level (tract and block) data used in the removal of Japanese Americans. In 2007 Margo Anderson and William Seltzer found Commerce Department records showing that the Bureau gave the Treasury, for the Secret Service, the names and locations of people of Japanese ancestry in the Washington, D.C., area. It did so seven days after a 4 August 1943 request from Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau. The records show no such lists for other parts of the country. Prewitt, Census director from 1998 to 2000, called the new evidence convincing.

sources.quote: The Bureau previously has acknowledged that it provided neighborhood information on Japanese-Americans for that purpose, but it has maintained that it never provided "microdata," meaning names and specific information about them, to other agencies.
sources.note: Same article quotes Kenneth Prewitt, Census director 1998-2000: 'The [new] evidence is convincing'.

sources.institution: Social Research (William Seltzer and Margo Anderson)
sources.title: The Dark Side of Numbers: The Role of Population Data Systems in Human Rights Abuses
sources.quote: Despite accusations that microdata were released (Toland, 1982), the bureau has denied the charge and no definitive evidence to the contrary has emerged. Nevertheless, there now seems to be general agreement that the provision of mesodata and professional expertise violated the spirit, if not the letter, of the promises embodied in the census confidentiality laws (Prewitt, 2000).

It shows that the Bureau still denied releasing microdata in 2001, and that it had given the West Coast military authorities tract-level tabulations (January 1942) and census-block maps, also FOUND: 'making available census-block maps showing the number of Japanese American enumerated as residing in each block'.

issues: Wrong history in the correction. It says 'For decades the Bureau acknowledged releasing block-level data'. The opposite is true. The acknowledgement dates only from 2000: Anderson and Seltzer documented the tract and block data that year, and director Kenneth Prewitt apologised in 2000. SciAm opens with 'Despite decades of denials', and Seltzer and Anderson (Social Research 2001, p. 492) say the bureau 'has denied the charge' that microdata were released.

Overreach by omission. The correction does not say that the 2007 records cover only the Washington, D.C., area. SciAm: 'The records, however, do not indicate that the Bureau was asked for or divulged such information for Japanese-Americans in other parts of the country.' Added, so readers do not infer that name lists were used for the West Coast removal.
Typo: 'an 4 August 1943' should be 'a 4 August 1943'. The request came from Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau, which is now named.

The FALSE verdict on the claim 'never names' stands.

myths.claim: IBM/Hollerith punch-card machines were how the Nazis found and identified the Jews they murdered.
myths.correction: Hollerith punch-card machines, made by IBM's German subsidiary, did tabulate German census data, including the 1939 census's “race” data. From 1942 they were used at the headquarters of the concentration-camp system to track living prisoners, especially their occupational skills. But the US Holocaust Memorial Museum stresses that locating and identifying victims “did not rely on modern technology”. That was done with paper records (Jewish community lists, church, tax and police records, compulsory self-registration) and with local knowledge and denunciation. About 4.5 million of the 6 million Jews killed lived in Poland, the Baltics and the Soviet Union, where such machines would not have been found. In the occupied Netherlands, the population register and its identity cards played an important role in rounding Jews up. Edwin Black's IBM and the Holocaust (2001) argues for a larger role for the machines.

The Bundesarchiv essay on those cards (Zimmermann) says their use for the deportations 'could not be proved so far ... and is rather unlikely', because the cards reached the registration offices only in April/May 1941 and the Reich Office of Genealogy in January 1942.
